notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0105.stoa009.opp-la: Preface: 'poet Sarazanium' read as 'post'; 'nidi' in I read as 'nisi'; 'gemis' read as 'genus'. 'quam mecum luderet' read as 'quam [si] mecum luderet'. Letter I's consular date (Gratian and Cyricius) is part of the forgery and does not correspond to a real consulship pairing. In V the sense of 'ad tempus diuque' is obscure; rendered loosely. In I 'profanorum hominum' is odd (perhaps for 'omnium hominum'); translated as it stands.

Evident scanning errors read as: accurati = accusati, cextra = extra, placete = placere, assisiit = assistit, vot = vos, catus = coetus, vebis = vobis, agal = agat, quie ... Patron = quae ... Patrum, creditor = creditur. 'Oportet negligentes propulsare' is odd in sense (perhaps 'nocentes' was meant); translated as printed. 'Sub metu irrefragabili auctoritate' is awkward and rendered literally. The dating by the consuls Flavianus and Stilicho (AD 400?) postdates Damasus (d. 384), consistent with the letter being a forgery.

Line 3: 'mirari tamen non possumus vestram solertiam' is awkward; rendered as admiration ('cannot but admire'), though literally 'we cannot wonder at'. Several scanning errors corrected silently: 'licent' for licet, 'ordinali' for ordinati, 'nou' for non, 'quis (scio)' for quia, 'sunu' for sunt, 'neccsse' for necesse, 'allero' for altero. 'Absolute instituti' refers to absolute ordination, i.e. without assignment to a particular church or title. The passage on 'episcoporum' as a genitive plural turns on Latin grammar; 'of bishops' preserves the argument.

Several evident scanning or printing slips were read as intended: 'sim' as 'sint', 'habeam' as 'habeant', 'praedicit' as 'praedicti', 'abeo' as 'ab eo', and 'pon' as 'non'. In 'nec ... consentiat sacerdotum', 'sacerdotum' is taken with 'nullus' (no one of the priests). 'Formatae' are canonical letters of commendation. The sentence beginning 'Nor shall we be true disciples' is syntactically tangled in the Latin and is rendered according to its evident sense. The consular date 'Libius and Theodosius' does not correspond to any real consulship and belongs to the forgery.

Letter IV: 'perscripta' read as 'per scripta'; 'vocali' read as 'vocati'. 'His, qui dati sunt...' is syntactically confused; rendered loosely. Letter IV's heading mentions referral of cases to the apostolic see, which the letter text does not treat. Letter V: the Latin is ungrammatical (e.g. 'imbuere' lacks a governing verb); 'indago' rendered 'evidence', uncertain. The list of names of the Seventy is garbled and the names cannot be securely identified. 'Bethsarda' read as Bethsaida; 'Jobii' rendered as Jonah, as the usual tradition has it.

nodes.text: THE APOCRYPHAL WORKS OF SAINT DAMASUS.
TO THE READER.

I had decided to dismiss the apocrypha; but since some profit and use may at times be had from the letters, and the bookseller wished it of me, I have allowed them to be added to the genuine minor works of Damasus. For those addressed to Stephen and the bishops of Mauretania, to Prosper and the bishops of Numidia, to Aurelius of Carthage, and to the bishops of Italy, have already been shown to have come out of the workshop of Isidore Mercator, by Labbe in his Collection of the Councils and by Coustant in the Preface to the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 145, to pass over others. As for those to Jerome, Erasmus rightly complains that a man could have been so shameless as to dare to attribute them to Damasus; on this matter Schelstrate, dissertation 2, chapter 3, may be consulted. I could not, however, be brought to keep the decrees that circulate under his name: for since Coustant, after Sarazanio and Crabbe, has again diligently collected them all in the work he entitled 'Censure of the Decrees Ascribed to Damasus', and has brought forward truly weighty reasons why they falsely claim the name and authority of that pontiff, the reader will spend his effort far better in consulting that learned man than in trifling with me.
FIRST LETTER.
Damasus to his most reverend brother and fellow bishop Aurelius.

We have received the writings of Your Holiness with due veneration, and from them we have learned that your reverence and prudence thirst (as was fitting) for the apostolic institutions. On this account we have sent some of the things you asked for; and others we wish to send when you send again. Yet from the end of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have passed over none of our predecessors from whose statutes we have not sent you something, under certain seals, by the presbyter Ammonius and the deacon Felix. These we desire both that you keep and we command that they be preached and published to others, so that they may be kept inviolate by all with due veneration, and observed inviolate, and diligently venerated by all in all times to come: because wilful violators of the canons are severely judged by the holy Fathers, and condemned by the Holy Spirit (by whose prompting and gift they were dictated); since those are not unfittingly seen to blaspheme the Holy Spirit who, not compelled by necessity but willingly (as was said above), either wantonly do, or presume to say, anything against these same holy canons, or freely consent to those who wish to do so. For such presumption is plainly one kind of those who blaspheme the Holy Spirit: since (as has already been touched on) it acts against him by whose impulse and grace these same holy canons were issued. Diabolical wickedness, indeed, is wont to deceive many subtly; and it very often so mocks the imprudence of some by a semblance of piety as to persuade them of harmful things in place of wholesome ones. Therefore the rule of the holy canons, which were framed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, must be faithfully known and diligently handled by us; lest in any way, without unavoidable necessity, we transgress (God forbid) the statutes of the holy Fathers: but walking most faithfully by them, may we deserve, with the Lord's help, through their merits, to have the glory of reward and the fullness of labour together with those who framed them by divine prompting. These things having thus been duly deliberated, and the deliberation having been brought to the notice of your Churches, it is above all fitting that you obey the rules of these same holy canons, lest the sloth of some cause anyone to oppose them in any matter: but may your wise and sound teaching, which desires that you please God in all things, show you to be faithful fellow workers, co-heirs and fellow partakers with them of the heavenly kingdom in its seats. Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, Gratian and Cyricius, most distinguished men, being consuls.
LETTER II.

Damasus, servant of the servants of God, and by his grace bishop of the holy catholic Church of the city of Rome, to Stephen, archbishop of the council of Mauretania, and to all the bishops of the African province. Having read the letter of your fraternity, first I give thanks that I have deserved to enjoy the blessing of such great brothers; next, that I have found you solicitous for the brothers, and bearing with them the cross of the Lord, who says: Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me, and the rest pertaining to this. Therefore, since in the present consultation on these proceedings your beatitude, moved, opportunely, in its apostolic heart, has urged us to extend protection to the brothers by apostolic authority and to come to the aid of their wrongs, since it is clear that you say compassionately with the Apostle: Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is made to stumble, and I do not burn? taking pains that none of those entrusted to you be torn or seized by savage beasts: for this reason it is fitting, according to your prudent admonition, but more according to the divine command of the Lord, that we, who have received the episcopal ministry over his house, that is, the universal catholic Church, should keep careful watch; lest any of his sacred gifts, that is, apostolic men, successors of the apostles, and ministers, can be suppressed while we sleep, and condemned unjustly and without consulting us.

I. You know, dearest brothers, that the apostolic see has been established as the foundation fixed by God and immovable, and the most shining title of his priests, that is, of all bishops, and the summit of the Churches. For you are (as the divine Word truly declares) Peter, and upon your foundation the pillars of the Church, by which bishops are understood, have been established: and to you I have committed the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and have proclaimed [your] power to bind and loose the things that are in heaven and those on earth. You stand as prince and teacher of the orthodox and immaculate faith for profane men, and for my members, and above all for my disciples; in whose stead today, by the grace of God, we discharge an embassy for Christ, and all the prelates of this holy see have acted, act, and will act in his stead. Therefore I would command that all the things you have made known are not permitted, did I not know you to be so fully instructed that you do not doubt that all the things about which you consult are unlawful.

II. For it is lawful for the metropolitan, together with all his comprovincials, so that none of them is absent and all agree in the affairs of each, to examine bishops and the major causes of ecclesiastical business: but it is by no means lawful to decide their major complaints and those of ecclesiastical causes, or to condemn bishops, without the authority of this holy see; to which all ought to appeal, if need be, and be supported by its aid. For (as you know) to hold a synod without its authority is not catholic: nor can a bishop be definitively condemned except in a lawful synod, assembled at its proper time by apostolic summons: nor are any councils ever read of as valid which were not supported by apostolic authority.

III. The accusers of bishops, and the witnesses, about whom you have asked, ought to be without any infamy, or suspicion, or manifest stain, and fully instructed in the true faith, and such as divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood: since (as ancient authority hands down) those who ought not and cannot be promoted to the same honour cannot accuse priests or testify against them.

IV. For the summons to a synod (according to the decrees of the Fathers) of the one who is impeached must be canonical, both in his own presence and also by letters and envoys, with a fitting and canonical interval: because unless he has been canonically summoned at his proper time and by canonical ordering, even if he has come to the assembly from whatever necessity, he shall in no way answer his ensnarers unless he willingly wishes to; since not even the laws of the world permit this to be done, how much less the divine laws.

V. As for those expelled and despoiled of their property, I can tell you nothing truer than what the holy Fathers have defined and our predecessors have confirmed by apostolic authority. For these things stand thus: the holy canons have decreed that bishops who have been expelled and despoiled of their property should first recover their own Churches, and that all their goods should be lawfully restored to them: and afterwards, if anyone wished to accuse them, they ordained that he should do so at equal risk, decreeing that the judges of bishops be bishops of right understanding and just will, meeting in church in due time and after a long while, when they [the accused] have recovered their strength and enjoy their property with full power, with their friends and wise men, servants of God, giving counsel, where there would be witnesses for each of those who appear to have been oppressed. And the rest pertaining to this order: which, avoiding prolixity, we have not inserted here, because we believe this suffices. But if anyone is not content with these, let him read them, and he will be satisfied. For we know that unarmed men cannot properly fight with armed men: so neither can those who have been expelled or despoiled of their goods properly go to law with those who stand in their rank and enjoy their friends and goods. Nor do the laws of the world permit this to be done to men of the world: rather they order those first expelled or oppressed or despoiled to be restored with all their goods, and afterwards, at the proper time, as their law contains, they direct them to come to the pleas; nor do they permit one who appeals to be confined by any custody of prison. For earthly things (as you know) teach in part what heavenly things are.

VI. But accusers and accusations which the laws of the world do not accept are in no way to be admitted in the cases of these [men], because the catholic Church defends everything that is irreproachable. And there is no doubt that this was laid down by our forebears because of the plots of wicked men. For it befits the priests of the Lord to handle the cases of their brothers piously and to attend to them reverently, and to set their judgements above sacrifices; and to carry everything through not insolently or with tyrannical domination, as is reported of certain men, but charitably, for God's sake and out of brotherly love: and what anyone does not wish done to himself, according to the Lord's word, let him not presume to inflict on another: and with the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you. But what we have received from the preaching of the Apostles and the instruction of the Fathers we ought always to hold; so that we may not seem to forge anything new, or to aim at harm to our brothers: but let us bear one another's burdens, so that, according to the Apostle, we may be able to fulfil the law of the Lord.

VII. For a suitable time ought to be provided for, when the case of each accused person may be brought forward most properly into the open, so that its weight and its consistency may in no way be found to be set forth against the decrees of the Fathers or the profession of the synods. Let all attend to it in due order, so that they may answer it reasonably in all points, and show plainly that they wish [to act] justly. But let no one be brought in in person [alone]: but let accusers and accused be heard on an equal footing, as the order of proceedings requires. And let accusers and judges not be the same, but accusers by themselves, judges by themselves, witnesses by themselves, accused by themselves, each in his own proper order. For let the written charge always come first, so that the false accuser may receive the like penalty; because before the written charge no one ought to be judged or condemned, since the laws of the world also retain these same things. In all these matters let true equity always be done, so that they may obtain the reward of accusation and judgement and testimony through the truth of the proceedings. For it is written: The Lord will abhor lying lips, and a false witness uttering lies, and one who sows scandals and quarrels among brothers, he himself warning and saying: You shall not slander your neighbour, nor oppress him by force. You shall not do what is unjust, nor judge unjustly. You shall not regard the person of the poor, nor honour the face of the powerful. Judge your neighbour justly. And what you do not wish done to you, do not do to another: and the rest. And above all, since we have the Apostle's precept, it is fitting to take heed to ourselves and to the flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed us as bishops, to rule the Church of God, which he acquired by his own blood. And again: Beware of the wolves, beware of the evil workers, who do perverse things and speak hostile things, so that they may always disparage and defame the disciples of the Lord: whom you and all the priests of the Lord ought to correct with the utmost zeal: because there is no worse evil than that citizens should envy citizens, and priests or clerics should plot against priests or bishops, as the voice of truth also testifies: Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye; and whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is better that a donkey's millstone be hung about his neck and that he be sunk in the depth of the sea. And likewise: Blessed is he who has not taken offence at me. Beyond doubt he has taken offence against God who gives offence to his bishop or priest. And many such things, which are not brought in here, lest the letter be made too long. You ought also to warn and instruct your aforementioned neighbours to withdraw from such men, and quickly to correct what they have unlawfully done against the aforesaid brothers. And those whom they have injured without consulting us, let them heal with full satisfaction, and quickly reconcile them to themselves, if they do not wish to incur the censure of the apostolic see. For if anything perhaps had arisen against them or concerning them, our examination should have been awaited, so that by our authority (as has always been the privilege granted to this see) they might be condemned, or be upheld by our help. For they ought not to have invaded our rights at their own pleasure, without the apostolic see's arrangement commanding it. From such men let all priests henceforth abstain who do not wish to be cut off by the censure of the Apostolic Rock (on which Christ, as was said before, built the universal Church, to which the highest judgements of bishops and the greater cases, as was mentioned a little above, are reserved and secured) and from priestly honour.

VIII. For a respite of six months, or longer if necessary, is to be granted to bishops accused in criminal cases: since no one versed in secular learning is unaware that this is permitted even to laymen: how much more to priests, who are without doubt their superiors. It is also found established in the decrees of the holy Fathers that it is not canonical to judge or condemn any of the priests before he has his accusers, canonically examined, present, and receives an opportunity to defend himself, that is, an ecclesiastical respite for clearing away the crimes and offences.

IX. Let the accusation for the first hearing not take place outside one's own province without apostolic instruction, to which reverence ought to be kept in all cases, since the ancient rule of the Fathers also teaches this, with which imperial statutes likewise agree. The examination of crimes, they say, is to be conducted where the crime was committed. For elsewhere the accused of crimes is forbidden to be heard. And elsewhere in the canons it is commanded: All matters are to be concluded in their own places, where they arose: and other such things like these: saving, however, in all things the apostolic authority, so that nothing in these matters be decided before it is known to please it, by which all ought to be supported. And if anything grave and intolerable should befall them, its censure is always to be awaited. For let no one, driven by insolence or by the goad of his own thoughts, and (as we know has often been done) presume to disparage or accuse any of the priests: because injury to them pertains to Christ, in whose stead they discharge an embassy on behalf of the people redeemed by Christ's blood. For we know that their cases, since they are God's cases, are to be reserved to the judgement of him who is able to kill the body and send the soul into Gehenna. He who says: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay. Before whom conscience is bare, from whom hidden things are not concealed. All are also to be instructed, since through us Christ has thundered to him, that it is not for the sheep but for the shepherd to foresee the plots of the wolf. The blessed apostle Paul therefore warns that judgement should not be presumed rashly and lightly concerning those whom no one can judge more truly or better than God: But you, he says, why do you judge your brother? or why do you despise him? For we shall all stand before the judgement seat of Christ. For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to the Lord. So each of us will give account of himself to God. In this, therefore, let no one take rash liberties upon himself, so as to do anything other than what pertains to concord, whereby the unity of the Church might be scattered. Let no one, then, lightly consent to the disparagement or judgement or condemnation of brothers, and especially of priests, who are nearer to God, and who make the body of Christ with their own mouth: Because for this the wrath of God comes upon the sons of dissension, who persecute Christ in his members. Do not, brothers, do not become partakers with them, nor share in the sins of such men, or in their unfruitful words. Rather, rebuke the gatherings of such men, who strive to stretch out their tongues like a bow against their brothers. Defend your brothers, then, and warn all to arm themselves against the persecutors of their brothers. But we are confident of better things concerning you, and nearer to salvation: because neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, as the teacher of the gentiles teaches, will be able to separate us from the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is perfected above all in priests and in his other members. Do not therefore throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For behold, the judge stands before the door, gladly promising crowns to those who for his sake bring help to their brothers, and aid the oppressed, and labour together in charity. But if anyone withdraws himself, he will not please God, but falls, because he did not lift up the one falling, but withered away. Let us not be of those who withdraw, to [our brothers'] oppression, but of those who support, to their gain and to the supply of the brothers. Therefore take up the armour of God, so that you may be able to resist all who presume in this way: and put on the breastplate of righteousness, with your feet shod in preparation of the Gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to quench all the fiery darts of the most wicked one. And take up the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the Word of God, rooted and grounded through all prayer and supplication, so that you may all say the same thing, and there may be no schisms among you, dividing the good and whole body of the Church into crooked novelties. The apostle therefore warns us no longer to judge one another rashly. For he judges rashly who condemns a bishop without the authority of the apostolic see: since (as was touched on a little above) this privilege has been specially reserved to it. But judge this rather, he says, that you not put a stumbling block or an occasion of offence before your brother. For plainly, by these and innumerable other testimonies of the decrees, it is manifest to all that a bishop ought not to be condemned, even though his reputation be examined, until the judgement of our apostolic authority concerning him, that is, of Peter the prince of the apostles, is known: inasmuch as he alone and before all was entrusted with, and was found worthy to receive from Christ God, the King of kings, the keys of the kingdom of heaven, to open to the faithful and to men well-disposed towards the same our Lord, and to shut to the unbelieving and ill-disposed, and to the assailants or injurers of his priests and of the holy Church, redeemed by his precious blood. Which indeed he has asked us also to do. Not that anything new is now commanded: but that what is transgressed through the sloth of some, either knowingly or negligently, may henceforth be observed by all: so that those things which have been established by apostolic tradition and that of the Fathers may always be held under fear, by irrefragable authority. For it is written in the second Epistle to the Thessalonians, and to Timothy, with the apostle warning: Stand firm, and hold your traditions, which you have learned, whether by word or by letter. Likewise elsewhere through the prophet: I also waited, as blessed Isaiah thundered, for them to do judgement: but they did iniquity, and not justice, but a clamour, troubling all the pious. And they ought to know this, that the judgement of God is according to truth upon those who do such things: although they despise the riches of God's goodness, and forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the kindness of God leads them to repentance; but according to their hardness and impenitent heart they store up for themselves wrath on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgement of God, who will render to each according to his works. And elsewhere it is written: I am the Lord your God: you shall not do iniquity in judgement. You shall not accept the person of a man, nor marvel at the face of the powerful. You shall keep away from every unjust word. You shall not attack the innocent and the just, nor kill [him]. Beyond doubt he does iniquity in judgement who claims for himself what he is not permitted to claim. Therefore let no one presume to usurp without its counsel the things that have been granted to this holy see, if he does not wish to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honour, as a despiser. So it is right to drive off the negligent, but in such a way that the guilty are not strengthened; and [it is right] for the good to resist the wicked or those who plot against their brothers, lest, overcome by the torpor of sloth, they be held guilty of silence. So whoever can oppose and disturb the perverse and does not do so, this is nothing other than to favour their impiety. For he is not free from suspicion of hidden complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime. But be perfect and whole in the same mind, and strengthened in the same knowledge: so that, directing your ways through it unswervingly to the same [end], you may come to the aid of all the oppressed, because the Lord is entrusted to you; coming to whom, a living stone, rejected indeed by men because of the impiety of such people, but chosen and honoured by God, upon whom you, as living stones, are built up in the Lord into a spiritual [house], into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices to him as a sweet savour. For it is a sacrifice very pleasing to the Lord to help all the oppressed: how much more those of whom he says: Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me, and so on. He indeed offers prosperity to the Lord who drives adversity away from the afflicted and oppressed. And now, brothers, we commend you to God and to the word of his grace, who is able to perfect and to give an inheritance among all the sanctified. May the God of peace and consolation himself grant you to be of the same mind towards one another, and in him always and in all things, so that with one accord, with one mouth and one heart, you may honour him in concord and in the help of your brothers, who is powerful to strengthen all and to console them according to his Gospel, and according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent in eternal times, but made manifest through the holy Scriptures and the teachings of the orthodox Fathers, according to the command of the eternal God, for obedience to the faith, in all things known to us, to the only wise God, our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom to the Father and the Holy Spirit be glory, honour, and dominion and power for ever and ever. Amen. May the Lord keep you always safe, dearest brothers. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Flavianus and Stilicho, men most distinguished.
LETTER III.
On chorepiscopi, and what they are, or whether they are anything or nothing.

To the venerable lords and brothers, Prosper, bishop of the first see of Numidia, Leo, Reparatus, Alexander, Benedict, Rufus, and all the other orthodox bishops everywhere who stand firm in the right, holy and apostolic faith, Bishop Damasus.

Although, dearest brothers, the decrees of the Fathers are known to you, we cannot but admire your diligence regarding the institutions of our elders, in that you do not cease to refer to us, as to the head, as has always been the custom, all things that can admit of any doubt: so that you may take answers from the place from which you received instruction and the rule of right living. Hence we also recall that you are not unmindful of the canons, which also command that this very thing be done. [You do this] not because anything of the rule of ecclesiastical knowledge is lacking to you, but so that, supported by the authority of the apostolic see, you may in nothing deviate from its rules. Therefore concerning the chorepiscopi, about whom you wished to consult us: what their ministry is, or what they are permitted to do, or what authority they have, or whether it is permitted for them to be made or not, since we have heard that they have already been prohibited; or what is to be done about those who are found already ordained: nothing seems to us a surer answer to give you than what we find was decreed long ago by our predecessors; namely, that for their pardon nothing at all else be reserved than the deprivation of the sacred ministry which they unlawfully assumed; because they had been prohibited both by this holy see and by the bishops of the whole world. Their institution, then, is exceedingly wicked, exceedingly perverse: because for these men to presume anything of the highest ministry of the priesthood lacks all authority, and is found to be contrary to the sacred canons, and a proud and superfluous arrogance tends to the disturbance of the whole Church: and whatever they have done in the aforesaid ministry of the highest priesthood is void and empty. That they are the same as presbyters is sufficiently established: because they are found to have been first instituted after the form and example of the seventy. But because (thanks be to God) they are not now necessary, as in the primitive Church, on account of the care which they were required to show towards the poor: and because they presumed unlawful things; and what they did was not validly done; and on that account many, falling into a false security, were frustrated and cheated of the ecclesiastical ministry: for this reason they have been removed from pontifical offices both by this holy see, as we mentioned above, and by all the bishops of the whole world. For (as has been reported to us) certain bishops, for the sake of their own ease, did not fear to commit their peoples to them: and so that they might do unlawful and prohibited things, these same men usurp for themselves the things which are owed to pontiffs alone; and the bishops themselves grow sluggish in their ease, and neglect the charge committed to them by God, though the Lord says: The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, and calls them by name, and knows his own, and his own know him. And likewise: As the Father knows me, I also know the Father, and I lay down my life for my sheep. And what he says of the hireling you know well: that he sees the wolf coming, and abandons the sheep, and flees, and the wolf seizes and scatters the sheep, and the rest. Through such men the care of the Church is neglected, and its condition is disturbed. And for this reason they have been prohibited; so much so that if any of them are found, they are to fall from their own rank. For those bishops who presume such things for themselves seem to me to be like harlots, who as soon as they give birth hand over their infants to other nurses to be brought up, so that they may the sooner be able to satisfy their lust. So these men too hand over their infants, that is, the peoples committed to them, to others to be brought up, so that they may satisfy their lusts, that is, so that at their own pleasure they may gape after worldly cares, and do more freely whatever each sees fit. Through such men souls are neglected, sheep perish, diseases grow, heresies and schisms spring up, churches are destroyed, priests are corrupted, and the other evils follow. The Lord did not teach thus, nor did the Apostles institute it: but let those who undertake the charge carry it out themselves, and themselves present their own sheaves to the Lord. For he himself diligently sought the lost sheep, he himself found it, he himself carried it back on his own shoulders, and he taught us thoroughly to do the same. If he himself had such care for the sheep, himself taught, himself tended, himself healed, himself carried back on his own shoulders, and loved so much that he even gave up his life for us (enduring many injuries, many reproaches, and many sufferings): what are we wretched and idle men going to say, who neglect even to spend care on the sheep committed to us, and hand them over to others to be brought up? These things must be corrected, brothers: for he who labours more will receive the greater reward. For we know of no more than two orders among the disciples of the Lord, that is, of the twelve Apostles and of the seventy Disciples: whence this third has come forth we are entirely ignorant. And what lacks reason must be rooted out. For that those are not bishops who have been ordained by fewer than three bishops is plain to all: since (as you know well) it has been prohibited by the holy Fathers that those who have been ordained by one or two bishops should even be called bishops. If they do not have the name, how will they have the office? For whatever they have done among bishops, or in matters pertaining to bishops alone, must (as has already been touched on above) be made void: because what they do not have they can by no means give: especially since none of the seventy Disciples, whose likeness these men bore in the Church before they were prohibited (as was mentioned above), is read to have assumed anything of what was owed specially to the Apostles and their successors. Nor in the law of the Lord, which is read to have been dictated to Moses by the Lord himself, did the sons of Aaron presume anything of those things which were specially granted to the high priests, that is, to Moses and Aaron. For no one doubts that Moses and Aaron alone, at the Lord's command, set up the altar in the Tabernacle of God, alone anointed, alone instituted priests by holy anointing, and did the other things that pertained to the high priesthood, of which one reads sufficiently in the divine Scriptures: since they were the high priests of the Lord, as is written of them: Moses and Aaron among his priests. So also now, since the shadow of the law has passed, and the light of the Gospel, by the grace of God, shines plainly upon us, those who bear the form of the seventy Disciples, in whose type namely the sons of Aaron were, ought to presume nothing of those things which belong to the high priests, that is, the bishops, whose figure Moses and Aaron held, just as those [sons of Aaron] did not touch anything of the ministry of the high priesthood. For that the chorepiscopi, before they were prohibited by the aforesaid ruling, were instituted after the form of the seventy, the canon sufficiently shows, where it says: The chorepiscopi also seem to be after the example and form of the Seventy: and the rest. Nor does it seem to us that we should pass over what is expressed elsewhere in the canons: Those who are called chorepiscopi in villages and estates, although they have received the imposition of hands of bishops, and have been consecrated as bishops, and so on. I judge that it is not said without reason, 'although they have received the imposition of hands of bishops'; since 'of bishops' contains in itself a plural number, and among the grammarians it is a genitive plural: for it seems to me that at that time they were ordained not by one but by several; for it would by no means say 'of bishops' if the ordination of such men were done by one, since 'of bishops' is said in the plural. But when it said 'chorepiscopus', it certainly meant a village bishop to be understood; and if a village [bishop], what is he doing in a city, when two bishops are altogether forbidden to be in one city? And if they have been established in a village and in a place where there were no bishops before, when a bishop is forbidden to be made even in a small city, or in a village, or a fort, and in absolutely all places where there were no bishops before, lest the authority and name of bishop be cheapened, what, I ask, will they be? See, neither does the place agree with the ordination, nor the ordination with the place: for if they received the imposition of hands of bishops, and were consecrated as bishops, where were they consecrated? For a village, since chora means village among the Greeks. And how for a village, if it is not permitted [for a bishop] to be made even in a fort or a small city? I ask you to explain: and if you cannot explain, as (I know) you cannot at all by reason or full authority, lay your finger on your mouth, and do not doubt that they lack all authority, namely because three things stand in the way by which their action or institution is annulled. One, that they are usually ordained by one bishop, in which their ordination disagrees with the canons, which command them to be instituted by the hands of bishops. Another, if they have been ordained by several bishops, and have been appointed either in a village, or in a fort, or in a small city, or altogether not in that place where bishops ought rightly to be made, or where there have not been [bishops] before, where the authority and name of bishop would be cheapened, or if in a city with another bishop: since (as was said before) two bishops ought not to reside in one city. The third, if they have been instituted absolutely, as we have heard of certain ones; all of which things altogether lack episcopal authority: and this further remains, that their order has no authority in the divine Scriptures: because (as was stated before) there are only two first orders in the Church, that is, of the Apostles and of the seventy Disciples. Indeed, if they are not bishops, because for the aforesaid reasons they cannot be bishops: and they do not wish to be called presbyters, because they aspire to be more; and they attempt to presume more than the seventy Disciples would have done (after whose form, as we touched on a little above, these men, before they were prohibited, were instituted by certain foolish men seeking their own things and not those of Christ Jesus), and presume to do unlawful and prohibited things; and they do not wish to be called what they are: I ask you to declare openly what they are: for either they are something, or nothing. For it is plainly evident that they are not bishops. And if they are not bishops, and scorn to be presbyters, what will they be? Either they will be something entirely, or nothing: because nothing can exist unless it has that from which it exists. And if it does not have that from which it exists, or from which it draws its origin, it neither has authority nor will be able to stand rightly, because it is empty, and it must be destroyed and fall, since it is nothing, and will be reckoned as nothing.

But if they are none of the things we have mentioned above, then it follows that they are none of the things that are owed to priests. And therefore they are not to be counted in the priestly catalogue either, except only (as we first recounted) that, out of mercy, to those who are willing to bear this humbly and do not aspire to more, and who confirm this very thing by a writing strengthened beneath with their own hand, this alone be granted: that they have a place among the priests, and be content with the ministry of presbyters, and be partakers of the Lord's table only. But those who wish to aspire to more are not to retain even this, that they be priests, but are to be deprived utterly of every ecclesiastical honour. For it is not lawful for them to consecrate priests, nor deacons or subdeacons, nor virgins, nor to set up an altar, nor to anoint or consecrate [it], nor to dedicate churches, nor to make chrism, nor to sign the foreheads of the baptised with chrism, nor indeed to reconcile any penitent publicly at mass, nor to send *formatae* [letters of commendation], nor to bless the people, nor to enter the baptistery or the sanctuary before the bishop, nor in the bishop's presence to dip or sign an infant, nor to reconcile a penitent without the instruction of their bishop; nor in his presence, unless he commands it, to confect the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ, nor with him present to teach or greet the people, nor to exhort the congregation; all of which you have been taught are owed to the bishops alone, both from what has been said above and from other decrees of the Fathers, or from the sacred canons. And if it is necessary for some who know less, they can be fully taught and instructed, so that by this both the distinction of grades and the summit of the dignity of the highest bishops may be shown. Let the same be held concerning presbyters too, that they do nothing without the command of their own bishop: for what is rare seems also to be more beautiful. And if the name of the bishops grows cheap, the whole condition of the Church is thrown into confusion. So in this matter the guilt is threefold: that they do prohibited things, that the sacred ministry is polluted by the cheapness of its sharing, and that the rights of the bishops (as far as the rashness of unlawful usurpation goes) are undone.

That it belongs to the proper office of the Apostles alone and their successors to confer the Holy Spirit, the book of the Acts of the Apostles teaches: especially since none of the seventy Disciples, whose likeness these men bear in the Church, is read to have conferred the gift of the Holy Spirit by the imposition of hands (as was said before). These things, then, since they lack all reason, let no one of the priests henceforth usurp or consent to, who does not wish to be separated from our priestly college. Nor let what is extinguished by us, and has already been extinguished by our predecessors and, as was said, by the other bishops of the whole world, be sown among some with dark roots: but let what is known to have sprouted wickedly be torn out by the roots, so that no tares may spoil the Lord's harvest. For thus the priests of the Lord will yield abundant fruit, if the things that are accustomed to kill the growing crop are cut away by the roots. Let it cease, then, let it cease, this presumption so many times prohibited and condemned: and let the high priests not imitate harlot women, who, for the sake of the pleasure mentioned, give their infants to others to nurse: but let them nurse [them] themselves, let them themselves render fruit with interest to their Lord, and present fruitful sheaves to him with glory. For if the Lord, among the other cares of his sheep, touched and cleansed lepers, why do we disdain to do the same? Or why do we, who have taken up the pastoral office, hand over [our sheep] to others to be fed? especially since the Lord said to Peter our teacher: If you love me, feed my sheep: and many other things similar to these. For the blessing which the aforesaid chorepiscopi used to give by the imposition of hands before their prohibition seems to us to inflict a wound rather than salvation. And those who did not have the summit of the episcopate, how could they give what they did not have? since there was nothing in the giver that the other could receive. Or who among men, even if we speak in human fashion, can give what he does not have? Especially since they were not bishops, they could not give what is owed to bishops alone. And therefore they rather wounded the heads which they touched by the imposition of hands, when they gave through some blessing what had not been conferred on them. And so whatever they presumed of the aforesaid pontifical ministries was void, and did no good to those touched: but rather, according to the prophet, they conferred a curse instead of a blessing (if it is right to say so). Wherefore, through that unlawful imposition of hands, as we touched on a little above, those who seemed to have received something had a wounded head. And where a wound has been inflicted, it is necessary to apply medicine by which the inflicted blemish may be healed: that is, what is not approved as lawfully done or conferred must necessarily be repeated, if it is to be complete. For how someone can retain an honour who received it from one who did not lawfully have the power to give it, I cannot find: since he who did not have the pontifical honour cannot bestow pontifical rights: nor could they claim for themselves that of which they were not capable, because of what had stood in their way. Claiming, then, the care of this examination especially for ourselves, we bestow mercy in such a way that, if perhaps any of these things have been committed, they may be corrected, that it may not be permitted to commit such things further, and that no excuse of ignorance may arise: for just as the condition of the Churches, established or adorned by wholesome arrangement, gives us cause for rejoicing, so it saddens us with no light grief whenever we learn that anything has been presumed or committed against the institutions of the canons or ecclesiastical discipline. If we do not cut these away with the vigilance we ought, we cannot excuse ourselves to him who willed us to be watchmen, if we do not keep his Church, which has been entrusted to us in general, pure, as far as we are able, from such unlawful superstitions: for we are not one flock and one shepherd otherwise than if, as the Apostle teaches, We all say the same thing: And let us be perfect in the same mind and in the same wisdom. Nor shall we be true disciples of the Lord otherwise than if each one hastens according to his strength to root out the root of bitterness springing up (as, you assert, it is now doing), so that it may not be able to harm or make the episcopal ministry grow cheap through their negligence, that is, of all the priests who have been set by him to tear out evils and plant better things: and if he who is to render account for his sheep to the eternal judge strives to cherish and rear them. If we desire to be disciples of the Lord, let us follow in his footsteps, so that it may be said of us: I am the good Shepherd, and I know my sheep, and I call them by name, and mine know me; and the rest. And again, at the admonition of the command of the Lord's voice, by which the most blessed apostle Peter is imbued by a threefold repetition of mystical sanctification, let him who loves Christ feed the sheep of Christ diligently and with great care: since we are constrained by love and reverence for that holy see, over which we preside by the abundance of divine grace, to avoid as far as we can the danger of so great a superstition, which (as has often been said) is propped up by no authority; lest the love of our blessed teacher Peter, the highest apostle, by which he testified that he was a lover of God, be found empty in us: since everyone who negligently feeds the Lord's flock so often entrusted to him is convicted of not loving the highest Shepherd, and of not wishing to become the disciple of him whose examples he neglects to imitate. For a far greater grace is acquired if the shepherd's solicitude offers the Lord profit from the sheep entrusted to him. For we remember that blessed Jacob too, who had served a long time for his wives, said: Twenty years I have been with you: your ewes and goats were not barren: I did not eat the rams of your flock, nor did I show you what was taken by a beast. I made good every loss: and whatever had perished by theft, you exacted from me: day and night I was burned by heat and frost: sleep fled from my eyes. If, then, he who feeds the sheep of Laban labours and keeps watch in this way, with how much labour and how many vigils ought he to apply himself who feeds the sheep of God. But in all these things may he instruct us who gave his life for his sheep; and may he help us, and grant that from those who have been entrusted to us we may bring back manifold fruit and an overflowing measure to eternal joys. And may so great a love of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, inflame you, that by your holy efforts you hasten with the utmost desire to restore to his sheepfold, to which all creatures have been handed over, all who stray in this way and presume unlawful and prohibited things: so that souls redeemed by the precious blood of Christ may not perish by their deception. It remains also [to say] that these men by no means entered by the door, because they had no door by which to go in: because (as was said) if they are not bishops, and aspire to be more than presbyters, by what door will they enter, since only these two orders are read of in the Church, and no further door lies open to the pastoral office by which a shepherd may enter? Hear, brothers, not me, but the Truth itself saying: He who does not enter the sheepfold by the door, but climbs up another way, he is a thief and a robber, and the rest. Since also the excellent preacher says: No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid: since only the two aforesaid foundations are found laid in the Church, whatever is found laid in addition to these can by no means stand. And therefore it must be torn out with all its foundations, actions and roots, so that it may no longer be able to sprout or germinate. Let not, then, this so often repeated speech beget weariness in you, brothers, or cause it: for it is of the utmost necessity that what, as we have learned from you, is so often unlawfully usurped be prohibited more often: and because truth, the more often it is stirred, shines the more into light: and what is warned against by repeating so often is less usurped. On these matters, indeed, much has already been said by our predecessors: by whom these men were once condemned and prohibited, just as they are now by us. Therefore, repeating it more often, we warn all to avoid things of this kind, and to keep away from such men, who do not wish to be made strangers to the priestly ministry together with them, as rebels. This we shall be able to prove only if you strive to root out such men, and not to favour them: and so thereafter the complaint about such a matter will cease, for whatever is so often usurped though forbidden is done out of a desire for insult. All these decretals, and the decrees of all our predecessors which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, we command must be kept by you and all bishops and by all priests generally, in such a way that if anyone offends against them, he should know that pardon will henceforth be denied him: since truth would come forward, if falsehood displeased. And rightly the case concerns us, who must hold the highest helm of the Church, if we favour error by silence. Given on the Kalends of June, Libius and Theodosius, most illustrious men, being consuls.
LETTER IV.

He orders that in future no one is to be judged by them through writings, but through a lawful accuser: and also that all cases to be judged are to be referred to the apostolic see. To all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy,
Damasus, bishop, greeting in the Lord.

I had wished, most beloved, out of the charity of our college, that all the priests of the Lord (as it was in the primitive Church) should be one heart and one soul, and persist in one devotion, and that none of the priests should be corrupted by favour towards or fear of worldly men, or depart in any way from the way of truth. But many things which can be corrected do arise, and the mercy of God surpasses the fault of those who offend: and for that reason vengeance is suspended, so that correction may have place. For it has been reported to the apostolic see that you receive accusations against brothers in writing, without a lawful accuser. This we forbid by apostolic authority to be done henceforth in the whole world, and what has lately been done we ask to be corrected without any delay: nor may it ever be permitted to examine the case of those who are accused through writings before they, summoned canonically at the plaintiffs' instance, come to a synod, and the one present truly learns and understands, through one present, what is charged against him. This is well said also through the wisdom of Solomon: Before you examine, do not reprove: understand first, and then rebuke. Before you have heard, do not answer. And although the reproof of opponents may be most evident, nevertheless for those who have been appointed to examine them, order must be kept by those who have been deputed to search into [matters] according to God, so that thus, with the work cooperating, we may find God also as witness, who says: Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst. For our Lord Jesus Christ also knew that Judas was a thief: but since he was not accused in person, he was therefore not cast out. Nor ought you in any way to do what he would not do. For the laws of the world require accusers who are present, and not absent ones through writings. Hence the canonical decrees of the fathers cry out not once but very often that no one can bring forward either accusations or testimonies through writings: nor may anyone give testimony about other matters, except those which are known to have been done in their presence. Likewise, whoever chooses to accuse another should accuse in person, by himself, and not through another, that is, with a written charge submitted beforehand. Nor should anyone ever be judged before he has lawful accusers present, and receives an opportunity of defending himself to wash away the charges. For care must be taken that anger does not steal upon anyone and make him do too quickly everything that is not lawful. May almighty God, as you keep these things and all the divine commands and apostolic precepts, protect you in all your acts by the extension of his heavenly arm, and lead you to the reward of the heavenly homeland with a manifold harvest of souls. Amen. Given on the third day before the Ides of April, Siricius and Ardabur, most illustrious men, being consuls.
LETTER V.
TO JEROME THE PRESBYTER.
Damasus, bishop, to his brother and fellow presbyter Jerome, greeting in the Lord.

When many collections of books had been brought to my judgement, it happened that I perceived my mind was eagerly held by the book of Psalms, and I [wished] to steep the memory of my capacity [in it]. I have considered, most loving brother and ever a priest in Christ, how, according to the Seventy translators and presbyters, that is, Matthias and Ptolemy, Muchius, Sacreus, Hydronius, Pamphylus, Zoastites, Didymus, Sanius, Epiphanius, Ciatres, Simon, and the rest, as far as our knowledge recalls, to find traces of the Seventy. I also ask your charity that, as you learned from your superior Alexander, our bishop, your fraternity may be pleased to send us the psalmody of the Greeks: for among us there is evidence of such simplicity that only on the Lord's day is one epistle of the Apostle read, and one chapter of the Gospel said: and neither the custom of psalm-singing is kept, nor is the grace of a hymn known in our mouth. I ask therefore, through our brother and fellow presbyter Boniface, that your Fraternity be pleased to open to us the traces of this matter. Sent on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, by Boniface the presbyter, to Jerusalem.
LETTER VI.
Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, to Jerome the Presbyter.

The Church rejoices, already satisfied from your fountain, and the curiosity of priestly times thirsts the more, so that what is worthy may be known, and what is unworthy rejected. Now the acts of the pontiffs which we were able to find through the zeal of our see, we have gladly sent to your charity. Pray for us, unto the holy resurrection, brother and fellow presbyter. Farewell in Christ our God and Lord. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, and received on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, sent from Rome to Jerusalem.
In the name of the Lord begins the series of the Roman pontiffs who have sat in the see of blessed Peter the apostle from him up to this time.
Blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, a Galilean by nation, from the village of Bethsaida, son of Jonah, brother of Andrew, etc.
